---
title: "Semester Project · Spine Rigor, Landscape Freedom"
---

**Teams of 2 · proposal due after L16 · final presentation in the last week.**

The course contract: you *master* L00–L14 and become *fluent* in L15–L24. The
project is where those meet. You pick a topic from the landscape — anything from
the second half of the course — but you execute it with the standards of the
spine: derivations checked, baselines run, claims backed by your own plots,
failures reported honestly.

**The one rule: a project is a question, not a demo.** "We fine-tuned a model"
is a demo. "How does LoRA rank trade off against full fine-tuning quality at a
fixed parameter budget?" is a question. Every proposal must state its question in
one sentence; every final report must answer it (including "the answer is no").

## Constraints (read these before dreaming)

- **Compute:** everything must run on a free Colab GPU (or equivalent). This is a feature — it forces small models, and small models are where understanding lives. If your plan needs an A100 for a week, shrink the model, not the rigor.
- **Scope:** ~30–40 hours per person across 8 weeks. A negative result obtained rigorously beats a positive result obtained sloppily.
- **Baselines are non-negotiable.** Whatever you build, there is a dumber thing it must beat — or you must explain why it doesn't.

## Suggested tracks

Pick one, adapt one, or propose your own (own proposals are encouraged and get
the same rubric).

| Track | The question | Spine skills it exercises |
|---|---|---|
| **LoRA fine-tune a small LM** | How does adapter rank (1, 4, 16, 64) trade against quality and trainable-parameter count on a small instruction/task dataset (GPT-2-small or similar)? | Backprop through frozen weights, parameter counting (HW2-style budget table), loss-curve reading |
| **Tiny CLIP from scratch** | Can a contrastive image–text model trained on a small paired dataset (e.g., MNIST/Fashion-MNIST + templated captions) do zero-shot classification? Where does it break? | Embeddings, cosine similarity, the InfoNCE loss derived and implemented, temperature ablation |
| **Speculative decoding demo** | How much wall-clock speedup does a small draft model give a larger target model, as a function of acceptance rate? Measure, don't quote. | Sampling distributions, the accept/reject correctness argument (derive it), KV-cache accounting (L23's numeric) |
| **Diffusion on a custom dataset** | Train a DDPM on data *you* assemble — 2D point clouds of your own design, audio snippets as spectrograms, pixel-art sprites. What does the noise schedule choice change? | Forward-process closed form (the L21 spine derivation), schedule ablation, trajectory visualization (HW4 skills, deeper) |
| **Mechanistic interp of a tiny transformer** | Train a 1–2 layer transformer on an algorithmic task (modular addition, sorting, parity). What did the attention heads and embeddings actually learn? | Attention by hand (HW3), reading weight matrices, designing probes — the most derivation-heavy track |

Other defensible directions: distillation (does a small model trained on a big
model's logits beat one trained on labels?), quantization (accuracy vs bits, measured
yourself), a DPO ablation on a toy preference dataset (L16's worked numeric, scaled up).

## Milestones

| Milestone | When | Format | Weight |
|---|---|---|---:|
| **Proposal** | week after L16 | 1 page: the question, the method, the baseline, the *minimum viable result* you'll show even if everything else fails, a compute estimate | 10% |
| **Mid-report** | ~4 weeks later | 2 pages: evidence of one end-to-end run (however small/bad), what surprised you, updated plan. The grade is for *de-risking*, not for results | 20% |
| **Final report** | last week | 4–6 pages: question, method, results with plots, honest limitations, "what we'd do with 10× compute" | 45% |
| **Presentation** | last week | 10 minutes + 3 of questions. Every team member presents; questions go to individuals | 25% |

The mid-report exists to kill the classic failure mode: 7 weeks of setup, 1 week
of panic. If your pipeline doesn't run end-to-end by the midpoint, the remaining
weeks rescue the *pipeline*, not the science.

## Rubric (final report + presentation)

| Criterion | Weight | Spine-level means... |
|---|---:|---|
| **Question & framing** | 15% | One-sentence question; falsifiable; placed against what the lecture/papers already say |
| **Technical correctness** | 25% | The core mechanism derived or verified (gradient check, allclose against a reference, a by-hand numeric — HW-style proof, your choice); no unexamined copy-paste at the heart of the project |
| **Experimental rigor** | 25% | Baseline present; seeds/configs reported; at least one ablation; curves explained, not just shown |
| **Honesty & analysis** | 20% | Failures reported with diagnosis (the HW2 ladder applies to research too); limitations section that names real ones |
| **Communication** | 15% | Report readable by a classmate; presentation answers "so what?" in the first minute; figures with labeled axes |

Note what is *absent* from the rubric: leaderboard performance. A team that shows
LoRA rank-1 surprisingly matches rank-64 on their task — with seeds, a baseline,
and a paragraph on why — outscores a team with a higher BLEU number and no analysis.

## Ground rules

- **LLM use** follows the [course policy](index.qmd#llm-policy): allowed as a tool, declared in the report (one paragraph: what you used it for, where it was wrong). The oral presentation is where we verify the understanding is yours — "I don't know, the model wrote that part" is the one unrecoverable answer.
- **Existing code:** you may build on public repos (nanoGPT, minGPT, HF PEFT...) — cite them, and the rubric's correctness row still requires you to *verify* the piece your question depends on, not trust it.
- One proposal revision is free; come to office hours before submitting, not after.
